feedback: If a learner picks 0.372 as larger because '372 > 38', line the decimals up tenths-under-tenths and compare the tenths first (3 vs 3, equal), then the hundredths (7 vs 8), so 0.372 < 0.38. Padding to 0.380 shows equal-length strings so the digit-count argument disappears.
If the grid shading surprises them — the 'shorter' 0.38 shades MORE squares than the 'longer' 0.372 — ask them to restate why: 0.380 > 0.372 because the deciding place (hundredths) has 8 > 7.
Reinforce by naming the deciding place aloud: 'they are equal in the tenths, so the hundredths decides.'
activities.intendedInsight: The length of a decimal does not determine its size; comparison is decided by the first place where the digits differ, read left-to-right. Trailing zeros make equal-length strings without changing value (0.38 = 0.380).
learnerActions: Write two decimals into aligned Ones . tenths . hundredths . thousandths rows, e.g. 0.372 and 0.38.
Pad the shorter decimal with a trailing zero so both have the same length: 0.38 becomes 0.380.
Compare left-to-right, place by place: tenths match (3 = 3), then at the hundredths the 7 and 8 differ, so 0.372 < 0.380.
State the comparison with the correct symbol and say which place decided it.
Shade each value on a thousandths grid (380 squares vs 372 squares) and check which covers more area.
Optionally, mark both decimals on a number line to hundredths/thousandths to see their relative positions as a second representation of the same comparison.
activities.title: Align and compare on a place-value chart

feedback: If a learner writes 5.62 for 'five and sixty-two thousandths', ask which place the word 'thousandths' names (the third place). The 2 must sit there, so 62 becomes 062: 5.062.
Check the reverse: ask them to read 5.62 and 5.062 aloud and notice these are different numbers (sixty-two hundredths vs sixty-two thousandths).
activities.intendedInsight: Naming a decimal by its place ('thousandths') tells you which column the last digit must occupy; a placeholder zero may be needed so the digits land in the correct places. 5.062 ≠ 5.62.
learnerActions: Read a decimal aloud using place-value names: 'five and sixty-two thousandths' rather than 'five point zero six two'.
Write 'five and sixty-two thousandths' as a numeral, anchoring the last digit in the named place: 'thousandths' means the 2 sits in the third decimal place.
Fill the places: 062 occupies tenths–hundredths–thousandths, giving 5.062.
Explain where the placeholder 0 goes and why it cannot be dropped.
Translate in both directions: given 5.062, say the words; given the words, write the numeral.
activities.title: Write spoken decimals keeping placeholder zeros

feedback: If the learner argues from digit count, redirect to the tenths-under-tenths alignment and ask which place first differs.
Accept a correct answer only with a place-value justification, not just the right symbol.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain a comparison in words — citing the first differing place — demonstrates place-value understanding rather than rule-following.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38, and prove it?'
Make a claim and justify it by aligning place values, not by counting digits.
Defend the claim against the 'longer-is-larger' bait by padding to 0.380 and comparing the hundredths.
Put the comparison into a sentence: '0.38 is bigger because they are equal in the tenths but 8 hundredths beats 7 hundredths.'
activities.title: Argue and justify a comparison (discussion)

feedback: For a comparison item, mark a digit-count answer wrong and prompt a place-value re-check with padded zeros.
For the ordering item, have the learner write all values to the same number of places first (0.300, 0.290, 0.305, 0.310), then order the aligned strings.
For the fill-in item, confirm the placeholder zero lands in the tenths place (5.062, not 5.62).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading, writing and comparing decimals can be verified across numeral and word forms and by ordering, including deliberately mixed-length cases that expose the 'longer-is-larger' trap.
learnerActions: Compare 0.372 and 0.38 and choose >, = or <, rejecting any answer based purely on digit count.
Complete 'five and sixty-two thousandths = ___' with the correct numeral (5.062).
Order four decimals of unequal length (e.g. 0.3, 0.29, 0.305, 0.31) by padding to equal length and comparing left-to-right, giving 0.29 < 0.3 < 0.305 < 0.31.
Explain each placement rather than only giving the final order.
activities.title: Check and order several decimals
